This is the result we have already used in univariate models and now we extend it to this multiple-equation case.



Here one can use the following general result that is related to the multivariate normal distribution. If (for some general matrices with suitable dimensions) \(\boldsymbol{Y} = \boldsymbol{X} + \boldsymbol{Z}\), where \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and \(\boldsymbol{Z}\) are independent and \(\boldsymbol{Z} \sim \mathsf{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\), then \(\boldsymbol{Y}|(\boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x})\sim \mathsf{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\).




Unless stated otherwise, hereafter likelihood function refers to this conditional likelihood function.





Note, however, that \(\mathsf{Cov}(\boldsymbol{u}) = \boldsymbol{I}_{T} \otimes \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\), which differs from the standard assumption of a linear model.
The reason why MLE still yields the OLS estimator has to do with the special structure of the regressor matrix \(\boldsymbol{\ubar{X}}\).
Later we will see that the result does not apply when the structure of \(\boldsymbol{\ubar{X}}\) changes. By direct calculation one can see that the subvectors \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}_{K}\) of \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\) are the standard OLS estimators based on the individual equations.




Extra: Covariance matrix estimation


Consider next the maximum likelihood estimation of the covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\). It is handy to first derive MLE for the inverse matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u^{-1} \equiv \boldsymbol{\Phi}\) and then (by the invariance property of the MLE) obtain the MLE for \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\) through the inverse \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\). Applying the parameter matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) and the short-hand notation \(\boldsymbol{u}_{t}(\boldsymbol{\pi}) = \boldsymbol{y}_{t}-\boldsymbol{X}_{t}^\prime \boldsymbol{\pi}\), we can write the log-likelihood as \[\begin{equation*}
    l(\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u) = \frac{T}{2}\log\left(\det(\boldsymbol{\Phi})\right) - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \boldsymbol{u}_{t}(\boldsymbol{\pi})^\prime \boldsymbol{\Phi} \boldsymbol{u}_{t}(\boldsymbol{\pi}).
\end{equation*}\]

Note that we have here simplified the derivation by (erroneously) not taking the symmetry of \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) into account. As noted in Appendix A, when we account for the symmetry correctly, the derivative becomes more complicated, while still the same likelihood equation is obtained for \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) and hence the same MLE. Intuitively, this is plausible, because the maximization results in a symmetric (and positive definite) solution, even if the symmetry condition is ignored.

Applying the derivation rules of Appendix A, we obtain \[\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Phi}} \boldsymbol{u}_t(\boldsymbol{\pi})^\prime \boldsymbol{\Phi} \boldsymbol{u}_t(\boldsymbol{\pi}) = \boldsymbol{u}_t(\boldsymbol{\pi}) \boldsymbol{u}_t(\boldsymbol{\pi})^\prime \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Phi}}\log\left(\det(\boldsymbol{\Phi})\right) = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u
\end{equation*}\] so that \[\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Phi}}l(\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u) = \frac{T}{2} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \boldsymbol{u}_{t}(\boldsymbol{\pi}) \boldsymbol{u}_{t}(\boldsymbol{\pi})^\prime
\end{equation*}\] Setting the right hand side to zero and replacing \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) in \(\boldsymbol{u}_{t}(\boldsymbol{\pi})\) by the above derived ML solution \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\) we obtain the solution \[\begin{equation*}
    \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\boldsymbol{y}_{t}-\boldsymbol{X}_t^{\prime} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\right) \left(\boldsymbol{y}_t-\boldsymbol{X}_t^\prime\widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\right)^\prime.
\end{equation*}\] Given that \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\) minimizes the log-likelihood function \(l(\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u)\), we can conclude on the basis of the invariance property of MLE that \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\) and \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u\) are (conditional) ML estimators for \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\).







The general maximum likelihood theory then implies that the estimators \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\) and \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u\) are asymptotically independent and the asymptotic distribution of \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\) is as in a situation where \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\) is known.




Extra: Some additional notes


The above result holds also without the assumption on stationary initial values provided the matrix \(T^{-1}\left(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u \otimes \boldsymbol{\Gamma }_{\boldsymbol{x}}^{-1}\right)\) is replaced by the general formula of the Fisher information matrix \[\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{\boldsymbol{I}}_{\boldsymbol{\pi} \boldsymbol{\pi}} (\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u) = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u^{-1} \otimes \sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathsf{E}\left(\boldsymbol{x}_{t} \boldsymbol{x}_{t}^\prime\right).
\end{equation*}\] The same point holds in the following where we consider restricted estimation and hypothesis testing (see below).

It is, however, useful to note that the accuracy of the asymptotic approximation in finite samples depends on the strength of the autocorrelation of the process.
When the stability condition of the VAR(\(p\)) is “nearly” invalid, the asymptotic approximation may be misleading in small (or even in fairly large) samples.





Details on this are available below as Extra material.




Extra: Estimation subject to linear constraints


Consider the VAR(p) model (from the previous section), where the parameters \(\boldsymbol{A}_{1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{A}_{p}\) (and possibly \(\boldsymbol{\nu}\)) are subject to linear constraints. Such restrictions can be expressed conveniently so that the parameter \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is assumed to satisfy \[\begin{equation}
    \boldsymbol{\pi} = \boldsymbol{H} \boldsymbol{\delta} + \boldsymbol{a},   
\end{equation}\] where \(\boldsymbol{H}\) is a known \(K(Kp+1)\times m\) matrix, \(\boldsymbol{a}\) a known \(K(Kp+1)\) vector and \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is an unknown \(m\times 1\) parameter vector. It is also assumed that \(\boldsymbol{H}\) is of full column rank, i.e., \(\mathsf{rank}(\boldsymbol{H})=m\).
It is quite common to express linear constraints by using the equation \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{R} \boldsymbol{\pi} = \boldsymbol{b},  
\end{equation*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{R}\) \((q\times K(Kp+1)\times m)\) and \(\boldsymbol{b} \,\, (q\times 1)\) are known and \(\mathsf{rank}(\boldsymbol{R})=q\). Using linear algebra one can see that the two ways are equivalent, when \(q+m = K(Kp+1)\). The former is useful when we consider estimation (in this section) and the latter is useful when we consider a Wald test (the next section).
Most commonly we are interested in situations where some of the parameters are restricted to be zero. For example, if we choose \(\boldsymbol{H} = [\boldsymbol{I}_{K^{2}p}:\boldsymbol{0}]^\prime\) and \(\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}\), then the last \(K\) components of \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) are assume to be zero so that \(\boldsymbol{y}_{t-p}\) has no explanatory (or predictive) power for the last component \(y_{Kt}\) of \(\boldsymbol{y}_{t}\). In this case, \(\boldsymbol{R} =[\boldsymbol{0}:\boldsymbol{I}_{K}]\) and \(\boldsymbol{b} = \boldsymbol{0}\).
The log-likelihood function for a restricted model is obtained by replacing \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) by \(\boldsymbol{H} \boldsymbol{\delta} + \boldsymbol{a}\). Denote \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{z}_{t} = \boldsymbol{y}_{t} - \boldsymbol{X}_{t}^\prime \boldsymbol{a} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{W}_{t} = \boldsymbol{H}^\prime \boldsymbol{X}_{t}.
\end{equation*}\] Then, the log-likelihood function \[\begin{equation*}
    l(\boldsymbol{\delta},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u)=-\frac{T}{2}\log \left( \det (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u )\right) -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}-\boldsymbol{W}_{t}^\prime \boldsymbol{\delta}\right)^\prime \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_u \left(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}-\boldsymbol{W}_{t}^\prime \boldsymbol{\delta} \right).
\end{equation*}\] Differentiate this function with respect to the parameters. As in the case of the derivative, we get \[\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\delta} }l(\boldsymbol{\delta},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \boldsymbol{W}_{t} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_u\left(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}-\boldsymbol{W}_{t}^\prime \boldsymbol{\delta}\right).
\end{equation*}\] Unlike in the case of \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\), the matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_u\) cannot be moved to the front of the sum. For this reason the equation \(\partial l(\boldsymbol{\delta},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u)\partial \boldsymbol{\delta} = \boldsymbol{0}\) cannot be solved without knowing \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), but instead the solution (usually) reduces to the form \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{\delta} = \left(\sum_{t=1}^{T} \boldsymbol{W} _{t} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_u \boldsymbol{W}_{t}^\prime\right)^{-1} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \boldsymbol{W}_{t} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_u \boldsymbol{z}_{t}.  
\end{equation*}\] Using the notation \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_u=\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) we can repeat the derivations from the previous section and conclude that the first order condition for \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\), i.e. \(\partial l(\boldsymbol{\delta},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u )\partial \boldsymbol{\Phi} = \boldsymbol{0}\), leads to the equation \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u =\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left( \boldsymbol{z} _{t} -\boldsymbol{W}_{t}^\prime \boldsymbol{\delta} \right)\left(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}-\boldsymbol{W}_{t}^\prime \boldsymbol{\delta}\right)^{\prime }.  
\end{equation*}\]
Given that the solution for \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) requires knowing \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\) and the solution for \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\) requires knowing \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\), numerical solution methods are required (except special cases). An illustrative method proceeds as follows. Replace the unknown \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\) by its unconstrained estimate \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u\) to yield \[\begin{equation*}
    \widetilde{\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{(1)} = \left(\sum_{t=1}^{T} \boldsymbol{W}_{t} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u^{-1} \boldsymbol{W}_{t}^\prime\right)^{-1} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \boldsymbol{W}_{t}^{-1} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u^{-1} \boldsymbol{z}_{t}.
\end{equation*}\] This then yields a new estimate \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u^{(1)}\), which can again be used to replace \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u\) in \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{(1)}\). This results in a new estimate \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{(2)}\) for \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\). This procedure can be continued until the estimates stop changing. This procedure is just an illustration. In practice, computer programs employ other algorithms. Nonetheless, the simple one step estimator \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{(1)}\) has good asymptotic properties, as it can be shown to be asymptotically equivalent to the true MLE (the reason being the orthogonality of \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\)).
Denote the ML estimators for \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\) by \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\delta}}\) and \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u\) and derive their asymptotic distribution by relying on the general theory of ML estimation. Differentiate the log likelihood function with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) once more (see the derivation results in Appendix A) to obtain \[\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\delta} \partial \boldsymbol{\delta}^\prime}l(\boldsymbol{\delta},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u)=-\sum_{t=1}^{T} \boldsymbol{W}_{t}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_u \boldsymbol{W}_{t}^\prime
\end{equation*}\] so that the Fisher information matrix for \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is \[\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{I}_{\boldsymbol{\delta\delta}}(\boldsymbol{\delta},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathsf{E} \left(\boldsymbol{W}_{t} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_u \boldsymbol{W}_{t}^\prime\right),
\end{equation*}\] which in the stationary case equals \(T \mathsf{E}\left(\boldsymbol{W}_{t}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_u \boldsymbol{W}_{t}^\prime\right)\). Similar calculations to those in the previous section show that \(\mathsf{E}\left(\partial^{2}l(\boldsymbol{\delta},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u)\partial \boldsymbol{\delta} \partial\sigma_{ij}\right)=0\) so that the parameters \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\) are orthogonal. Hence, the asymptotic distribution of \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\delta}}\) is \[\begin{equation*}
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\delta}} \overset{as}{\sim} \mathsf{N}(\boldsymbol{\delta},\mathcal{I}_{\boldsymbol{\delta\delta}}(\boldsymbol{\delta},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1}_u).
\end{equation*}\] Here we can account for the fact that \(\boldsymbol{W}_{t} = \boldsymbol{H}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{X}_{t}\), where \(\boldsymbol{H}\) is known and fixed, but this does not result in any more illustrative formula.
On the part of the estimator \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u\) for the constrained covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u\) it suffices to mention that it is consistent, which will be relied on later. Given what was noted above, we can write the estimator \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u\) as \[\begin{equation*}
    \widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}- \boldsymbol{W}_{t}^{\prime }\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\delta}}\right)\left(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}-\boldsymbol{W}_{t}^\prime\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\delta} }\right)^\prime.
\end{equation*}\]

8.3 Diagnostic checks
Residuals are also useful for investigating model adequacy. For an unconstrained model the residuals are defined by \[\begin{equation*}
    \widehat{\boldsymbol{u}}_{t} = \boldsymbol{y}_{t}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} - \widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}_{1} \boldsymbol{y}_{t-1}-\cdots -\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}_{p} \boldsymbol{y}_{t-p},\quad t=1, \ldots,T.
\end{equation*}\] The residuals should have similar properties to those of the theoretical errors \(\boldsymbol{u}_{t}\). To investigate this it is useful

to examine residual plots,
check whether there are individual or groups of “outliers”,
whether there are signs of changes in variance, or other clearly systematic features.

It is also often recommended to examine whether the residuals are (multi)normally distributed, although the asymptotic estimation and test theory does not entail normality of the error terms (\(\mathsf{iid}\) assumption suffices). i Empirical auto- and cross-correlation functions for the residuals may also reveal potential serial dependencies in the model errors. If \(\boldsymbol{u}_{t}\sim\mathsf{iid}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u)\), then the residual auto- and cross-correlations are asymptotically normal with mean zero. Unlike in the case of theoretical model errors, these are not asymptotically independent and the \(\mathsf{N}(0,1/T)\) approximation (for the one variable) does not hold.

The true asymptotic distribution can be derived, but is not considered in the course.
Some econometric programs (e.g., R) may print residual auto- and cross-correlations along with their true asymptotic standard errors or corresponding critical bounds that allow one to examine whether the residuals are serially dependent.

 
Portmanteau test. It is also possible to test for the presence of residual serial correlation. The so called Portmanteau test is directly based on residual auto- and cross-correlation functions (a multivariate extension of the Ljung-Box test). One version of it is \[\begin{equation*}
    Q_{H}^{\ast} = T^{2}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\frac{1}{T-h}\mathsf{tr}\left( \mathcal{\boldsymbol{S}}_{h}^{\prime }\mathcal{\boldsymbol{S}}_{0}^{-1}\mathcal{\boldsymbol{S}}_{h}\mathcal{\boldsymbol{S}}_{0}^{-1}\right),\ \mathcal{\boldsymbol{S}}_{h}
    =\sum_{t=1}^{T-h}\widehat{\boldsymbol{u}}_{t}\widehat{\boldsymbol{u}}_{t+h}^{\prime},
\end{equation*}\] where the null hypothesis is that there is no autocorrelation (here in the residuals) remaining. If the chosen unrestricted VAR(\(p\)) model error \(\boldsymbol{u}_{t}\sim \mathsf{iid}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_u)\), then \(Q_{H}^{\ast}\) is asymptotically \(\chi^{2}\)-distributed with degrees of freedom equal to \(K^{2}(H-p)\). If the model is restricted, the value of the degree of freedom of the \(\chi^{2}\)-distribution is \(K^{2}H\) minus the number of unrestricted autoregressive parameters. The asymptotic result entails that \(H\) is “large”.
Although there may be no reason to suspect residual (auto)correlation, the residuals might not be independent, as zero correlation is only related to linear independency.

In order to examine possible nonlinear dependencies (in a restricted sense) one can use auto- and cross-correlations based on squared residuals.



In this case, the usual standard errors and test statistics are not valid without appropriate adjustments.

 
Example (continued). Below, we report the fitted values of the VAR(2) model for \(rdif\) and \(dexch\). The plots also depict the residual time series along with their sample auto- and cross-correlation coefficients. The variation in the second residual series (\(dexch\)) appears to be slightly higher at the beginning, while the first residual series (\(rdif\)) exhibits some notable spikes. Despite these features, the residuals appear to be “reasonably random”. The auto- and cross-correlations of the residuals are generally small, with the exception of a few isolated spikes at higher-order lags.



























We employ the Portmanteau test (as discussed above) to check for remaining autocorrelation in the residuals. The results reported below show that the p-values exceed standard significance levels, indicating that the model specification is adequate (i.e., we fail to reject the null hypothesis of no autocorrelation at the conventional statistical significance levels).
In addition to checking for autocorrelation, we examine the distributional properties of the residuals. Plotting the histogram of the (standardized) residuals reveals a distribution with heavier tails than the normal distribution (leptokurtosis)—a feature hinted at by earlier graphical examinations (see the attached R code for plots not explicitly depicted here).

Furthermore, the slight correlation observed in the squared residuals at certain lags points toward conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH effects) and a consequent deviation from Gaussianity.
Overall, despite these distributional nuances, the model can be regarded as a reasonably successful specification.

H=6:Chi-squared = 21.248, df = 16, p-value = 0.1692

10.1 General idea of Granger causality
Consider two real-valued random variables \(x\) and \(z\). How should one define causality from the former to the latter variable? Without delving deeper to the philosophical implications, one can think that a necessary condition for causality is that the “cause” does not occur after the “consequence”. If \(x\) is a cause for \(z\), then one expects that \(x\) has predictive content for \(z\).
Let us formalize this intuition. Let \(x_{t}\) and \(z_{t}\) be real-valued stochastic processes and consider predicting the future values of \(z_{t}\) at time \(t\).
Let \(\Sigma_{z}(h|\mathcal{F}_{t})\) and \(\Sigma_{z}(h|\mathcal{F}_{t}\backslash \mathcal{F}_{t}^{x})\) be the corresponding mean square errors (MSE). We say that \(x_{t}\) Granger causes \(z_{t}\) if \[\begin{equation*}
    \Sigma_{z}(h|\mathcal{F}_{t})<\Sigma _{z}(h|\mathcal{F}_{t}\backslash \mathcal{F}_{t}^{x})
\end{equation*}\] for at least one \(t\) and \(h\in\{1,2,...\}\). That is, under Granger causality, we can obtain more accurate predictions for \(z_{t+h}\) (for some \(h>0\)) by exploiting information on the process \(x_{t}\).
If \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}\) and \(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}\) are vector-valued processes, the mean square errors become matrices. In this case, we say that \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}\) Granger causes \(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}\) if \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{z}}(h|\mathcal{F}_{t}\backslash\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\boldsymbol{x}})\neq \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{z}}(h|\mathcal{F}_{t})
\end{equation*}\] for at least for one \(h > 0\). The interpretation remains essentially similar: the history of \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) improves the prediction of \(\boldsymbol{z}_t\).

title: 10  Granger and instantaneous causality
text:
Let \(\mathcal{F}_{t}\) denote the information set (as already described in forecasting sections above) hypothetical variables set, which includes \(x_{t}\) and all other variables that are observed at time \(t\) and could be used to predict the future values \(z_{t+h},\ h\geq 1\).
The optimal (minimum mean square error) prediction of \(z_{t+h}\) given \(\mathcal{F}_{t}\) is denoted \(z_{t}(h|\mathcal{F}_{t})\).
Correspondingly, let \(z_{t}(h|\mathcal{F}_{t}\backslash \mathcal{F}_{t}^{x})\) be the optimal prediction of \(z_{t+h}\) when the history of \(x\), denoted by \(\mathcal{F}_{t}^{x}=\left\{ x_{s},s\leq t\right\}\), is removed from the information set.

title: 10  Granger and instantaneous causality
text:
10.2 Granger causality in VAR models
The information set \(\mathcal{F}_{t}\) applied in the general definition above is often infeasible in practice. In applied work, the information set is restricted to selected observed variables. Granger causality is most often studied in the context of VAR models, where the relevant information set consists of the components of the vector process and their lags.
Bivariate VAR model (\(K=2\)): Granger causality can be easily tested within a VAR model. Consider first, for simplicity, a bivariate VAR(\(p\)) process \[\begin{eqnarray*}
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
y_{1t} \\
y_{2t} \end{array} \right] =
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\nu_{1} \\
\nu_{2} \end{array} \right]
+
\sum_{j=1}^{p}
\left[ \begin{array}{cc}
a_{11,j} & a_{12,j}  \\
a_{21,j} & a_{22,j}  \end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
y_{1, t-j} \\
y_{2, t-j} \end{array} \right] +
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
u_{1t} \\
u_{2t} \end{array} \right].
\end{eqnarray*}\] If \[\begin{equation*}
a_{12,j}=0, \, j=1,2, \ldots, p,
\end{equation*}\] then the lags of \(y_{2t}\) do not help to predict \(y_{1t}\) and there is no Granger causality from \(y_{2t}\) to \(y_{1t}\) (that is, \(y_{2t}\) is not Granger-causal for \(y_{1t}\)).

That is, the restriction \(a_{12,1} = a_{12,2} = \cdots = a_{12,p} = 0\) implies the absence of such a Granger causality relationship.

When working with an estimated VAR model (for the empirical data), this hypothesis can be tested by the Wald or likelihood ratio (LR) test, following a \(\chi^2_p\)-distribution under the null hypothesis.

At times, such as in the vars package in R, the \(F\)-test statistic is used instead of the Wald test statistic, but the logic is the same.

 
Larger VAR models (\(K > 2\)) and indirect effects: When the VAR model contains more than two variables, Granger causality between two specific variables cannot always be tested by testing zero-restrictions in a simple pairwise manner. Consider the following three-variable VAR process: \[\begin{eqnarray*}
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
y_{1t} \\
y_{2t} \\
y_{3t}
\end{array} \right] =
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\nu_{1} \\
\nu_{2} \\
\nu_{3} \end{array} \right]
+
\sum_{j=1}^{p}
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}
a_{11,j} & a_{12,j} & a_{13,j}  \\
a_{21,j} & a_{22,j} & a_{23,j} \\
a_{31,j} & a_{32,j} & a_{33,j} \\
\end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
y_{1, t-j} \\
y_{2, t-j} \\
y_{3, t-j}
\end{array} \right] +
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
u_{1t} \\
u_{2t} \\
u_{3t}
\end{array} \right].
\end{eqnarray*}\] If, for instance, \(a_{12,1}= \cdots = a_{12,p} = 0\), the lags of \(y_{2t}\) do not help forecasting \(y_{1t}\) one period ahead. However, because the lags of \(y_{2t}\) may affect \(y_{3t}\), which in turn affects \(y_{1t}\), the lags of \(y_{2t}\) may help forecasting \(y_{1,t+1}\), \(y_{1,t+2}\) etc. In other words, there may be Granger causality through indirect effects.
 
General condition. Generally, we can consider Granger causality from one group of variables to another. Consider a stationary VAR(\(p\)) process and partition \(\boldsymbol{y}_t = [\boldsymbol{y}_{1t}^{\prime} \quad \boldsymbol{y}_{2t}^{\prime}]^{\prime}\), where \(\boldsymbol{y}_{1t}\) is \(K_1 \times 1\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}_{2t}\) is \(K_2 \times 1\) , (\(K_1+K_2= K\)), and write the VAR(\(p\)) process \[\begin{eqnarray*}
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\boldsymbol{y}_{1t} \\
\boldsymbol{y}_{2t} \end{array} \right] =
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\boldsymbol{\nu}_1 \\
\boldsymbol{\nu}_2 \end{array} \right]
+
\sum_{j=1}^{p}
\left[ \begin{array}{cc}
\boldsymbol{A}_{11,j} & \boldsymbol{A}_{12,j}  \\
\boldsymbol{A}_{21,j} & \boldsymbol{A}_{22,j}  \end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\boldsymbol{y}_{1, t-j} \\
\boldsymbol{y}_{2, t-j} \end{array} \right] +
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{1t} \\
\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{2t} \end{array} \right].
\end{eqnarray*}\] Here \(\boldsymbol{A}_{\cdot \cdot,j}\) are matrices. It intuitively seems that Granger causality from \(\boldsymbol{y}_{2t}\) to \(\boldsymbol{y}_{1t}\) relates to whether \(\boldsymbol{A}_{12,j}\neq \boldsymbol{0}\) for some \(j\). In other words, variables in \(\boldsymbol{y}_{2t}\) does not Granger cause \(\boldsymbol{y}_{1t}\), if and only if \(\boldsymbol{A}_{12,j}=\boldsymbol{0}\) for all \(j=1,...,p\).
 

Extra: More details for Granger causality


For simplicity assume \(p=1\) and denote \(\boldsymbol{A}_{ij,1}=\boldsymbol{A}_{ij}\). The general version follows similar logic.
Assume \(\boldsymbol{A}_{12}=\boldsymbol{0}\). Then the equation above implies a stationary VAR(1) presentation for \(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}\): \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{z}_{t}=\boldsymbol{A}_{11}\boldsymbol{z}_{t-1}+\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{t}.
\end{equation*}\] It follows that the conditional expectation depends only on the history of \(\boldsymbol{z}\): \[\begin{equation*}
    \mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{z}_{t+h}|\boldsymbol{z}_{s},\ s\leq t)=\boldsymbol{A}_{11}\mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{z}_{t+h-1}|\boldsymbol{z}_{s},\ s\leq t),\ \ h\geq 1.
\end{equation*}\] On the other hand, when \(\boldsymbol{A}_{12}=\boldsymbol{0}\), the full model implies: \[\begin{equation*}
    \mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{z}_{t+h}|\boldsymbol{y}_{s},\ s\leq t)=\boldsymbol{A}_{11}\mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{z}_{t+h-1}|\boldsymbol{y}_{s},\ s\leq t),\ \ h\geq 1.
\end{equation*}\] Comparing these two recursions (starting from \(\mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{z}_{t+1}|\cdot) = \boldsymbol{A}_{11}\boldsymbol{z}_t\)), one observes by induction that the predictions are identical for all \(h\) and \(t\). Hence, there is no Granger causality.
Now, assume \(\boldsymbol{A}_{12}\neq \boldsymbol{0}\). As \(\boldsymbol{u}_{t+1}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}_{s},s\leq t\), are independent, we have \(\mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{u}_{t+1}|\boldsymbol{y}_{s},\ s\leq t)=\boldsymbol{0}\) and the model yields: \[\begin{align*}
    \boldsymbol{z}_{t+1}-\mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{z}_{t+1}|\boldsymbol{y}_{s},\ s\leq t) &= \boldsymbol{z}_{t+1}-\boldsymbol{A}_{11}\boldsymbol{z}_{t}-\boldsymbol{A}_{12}\boldsymbol{x}_{t} \\
    &= \boldsymbol{\zeta}_{t+1}.
\end{align*}\] However, projecting only on the history of \(z\): \[\begin{align*}
    \boldsymbol{z}_{t+1}-\mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{z}_{t+1}|\boldsymbol{z}_{s},\ s\leq t) &= \boldsymbol{z}_{t+1}-\boldsymbol{A}_{11}\boldsymbol{z}_t-\boldsymbol{A}_{12}\mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{x}_t|\boldsymbol{z}_t, \ s \leq t) \\
    &= \boldsymbol{\zeta}_{t+1}+\boldsymbol{A}_{12}[\boldsymbol{x}_t-\mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{x}_t|\boldsymbol{z}_s, \ s\leq t)].
\end{align*}\] The last term is non-zero because \(\boldsymbol{A}_{12}\boldsymbol{x}_{t}\) is not a function of the history of \(\boldsymbol{z}\) alone. Thus, the mean square error (covariance matrix of the prediction error) differs between the two information sets. It follows that \(\boldsymbol{x}\) Granger causes \(\boldsymbol{z}\). \(\square\)

 
The “no Granger causality” hypothesis corresponds to \(K_1 K_2 p\) zero restrictions: \[\begin{equation*}
H_0: \boldsymbol{A}_{12,1} = \boldsymbol{A}_{12,2} = \cdots = \boldsymbol{A}_{12,p} = \boldsymbol{0}.
\end{equation*}\] This hypothesis can be tested using Wald or Likelihood Ratio (LR) tests.

Under the null hypothesis, these test statistics are asymptotically \(\chi^2_{K_1 K_2 p}\)-distributed.
Large values of the test statistic lead to rejection of the null hypothesis (i.e., finding evidence of Granger causality).
As mentioned, the \(F\)-test is also commonly used in finite samples (e.g., in R/RStudio).

 
Example: Three-variable process. Consider the VAR(1) process: \[\begin{equation*}
\boldsymbol{y}_t = \left[ \begin{array}{c}
y_{1t} \\ y_{2t} \\ y_{3t}   \end{array} \right] =
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
0 \\ 2 \\ 1   \end{array} \right] +
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}
0.5 & 0 & 0 \\
0.1 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\
0 & 0.2 & 0.3
\end{array} \right] \boldsymbol{y}_{t-1} +\boldsymbol{u}_t.
\end{equation*}\] Partitioning \(\boldsymbol{y}_t = [y_{1t} \quad \boldsymbol{y}^{\prime}_{2t}]^{\prime}\) so that \(\boldsymbol{y}_{2t} = [y_{2t} \quad y_{3t}]^{\prime}\).

Here, the sub-matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}_{12}\) corresponds to the top-right block \([0 \quad 0]\). Since this is zero, \(\boldsymbol{y}_{2t}\) (variables \(y_{2t}\) and \(y_{3t}\)) does not Granger cause \(y_{1t}\).
On the other hand, looking at the coefficients affecting \(y_{2t}\) (the second row), the coefficient for \(y_{1,t-1}\) is \(0.1 \neq 0\). Thus, \(y_{1t}\) Granger causes \(\boldsymbol{y}_{2t}\).

 
Granger causality when involving \(I(1)\) variables. Standard Granger causality tests (such as using F or Wald tests in a standard VAR), as above, rely on the assumption that variables are stationary (\(I(0)\)).

If you apply standard tests to non-stationary \(I(1)\) variables, the test statistics will not follow standard asymptotic distributions (like \(\chi^2\) or \(F\) distributions).
This often leads to “spurious causality”—finding relationships where none exist.

Different scenarios:

Scenario A: Variables are \(I(1)\) and cointegrated. If variables share a long-run equilibrium (cointegration), you must use a Vector Error Correction Model (VECM). Cointegration and VECM will be introduced in the next section.
Scenario B: Variables are \(I(1)\) and not cointegrated. If variables are non-stationary and have no long-run relationship, you must difference them. Using differenced time series, the limitation is that tests test short-run causality only. Long-run information is removed by differencing (but this is acceptable since no long-run relationship exists).
Scenario C: The robust and preferred solution is the Toda-Yamamoto (TY) procedure, which is valid regardless of whether the variables are \(I(0)\), \(I(1)\), or cointegrated. It avoids the potential biases associated with pre-testing for cointegration. The core idea is to estimate a VAR in levels (not differences) but add extra lags to “fix” the asymptotic distribution of the Wald test statistics. Steps:

Select lag length (\(p\)): Determine the optimal lag length \(p\) for the VAR using, for example, information criteria (AIC, SC, or HQ).
Determine integration order (\(d_{max}\)): Identify the maximum order of integration for the variables in the system (usually \(d_{max}=1\) for (economic) time series).
Estimate augmented VAR: Estimate a VAR in levels with a total lag length of \(p + d_{max}\).
Perform Wald Test: Test the Granger causality restrictions only on the first \(p\) lags. The coefficients for the extra \(d_{max}\) lags are ignored; they function essentially as nuisance parameters to ensure the test statistic follows a standard \(\chi^2\) distribution. Therefore, the test regression for a bivariate system where we test if \(\boldsymbol{x}\) Granger-causes \(\boldsymbol{y}\):

\[\begin{equation*}
  \boldsymbol{y}_t = \boldsymbol{\nu} + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \boldsymbol{A}_i \boldsymbol{y}_{t-i} + \underbrace{\sum_{j=p+1}^{p+d_{max}} \boldsymbol{A}_j \boldsymbol{y}_{t-j}}_{\text{ignored lags}} + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \boldsymbol{B}_i \boldsymbol{x}_{t-i} +   \underbrace{\sum_{j=p+1}^{p+d_{max}} \boldsymbol{B}_j \boldsymbol{x}_{t-j}}_{\text{ignored lags}} + u_t
\end{equation*}\] and test the hypothesis \[\begin{equation*}
H_0: \boldsymbol{B}_1 = \boldsymbol{B}_2 = \cdots = \boldsymbol{B}_p = \boldsymbol{0}.
\end{equation*}\]

11  Cointegration
text:
The vector \([1 \quad -\delta]^{\prime}\) is called the cointegration vector.
Long-run equilibrium: Cointegration is often interpreted as a long-run relationship. If the equilibrium is defined by \(y_{1t} = \tilde{\delta} y_{2t}\), then \(z_t\) represents the “equilibrium error”—the extent to which \(y_t\) deviates from its equilibrium value.
Because \(z_t \sim I(0)\), this error fluctuates around zero with constant variance. On average, the system remains in equilibrium.




The vector \(\boldsymbol{y}_{t}\) is effectively \(I(1)\), but differencing the entire vector is unnecessary for the second component.





Note that this definition allows for trivial cases (like the overdifferencing example above) where \(\boldsymbol{\beta} =(0,...,1,...0)\), meaning one variable is already stationary.
There can be several linearly independent CI-vectors. If there are \(r\) such vectors, they form the cointegrating matrix \(\boldsymbol{\beta} = [\boldsymbol{\beta}_{1}\ \cdots \ \boldsymbol{\beta}_{r}]\), and \(r\) is the cointegration rank.




Individually, \(y_{1t}\) and \(y_{2t}\) are \(I(1)\) because they both contain \(\tau_t\). Therefore, the time series they generate wandering behavior over time with increasing variance.
The non-stationarity of the processes \(y_{1t}\) and \(y_{2t}\) is driven by a one-dimensional random walk \(\tau_t\). However, the linear combination: \[\begin{equation*}
y_{1t} - b y_{2t} = (\mu_{1}-b\mu_{2}) + (\xi_{1t}-b\xi_{2t})
\end{equation*}\] eliminates the random walk \(\tau_t\). The result is stationary (even iid), and it does not behave like \(y_{1t}\) and \(y_{2t}\). Instead, it is fluctuating around the constant mean \(\mu_{1}-b\mu_{2}\). Thus, the process is cointegrated with the cointegration vector \((1, -b)\).
This implies that the linear combination \(y_{1t} - b y_{2t}\) (where \(b \neq 0\)) establishes a very strong linear dependence between the processes \(y_{1t}\) and \(y_{2t}\), forcing them to move ‘’hand in hand’’. This is perhaps most evident when \(b = 1\) and \(\mu_1 = \mu_2\), in which case the linear combination \(y_{1t} - y_{2t}\) is stationary with an expected value of zero.
Although the processes \(y_{1t}\) and \(y_{2t}\) wander wildly over time, cointegration prevents them from drifting too far apart.



Figure: A simulated cointegrated process (as above) where \(T=200\), \(\mu_1=\mu_2=0\), \(b=0.9\), \(\sigma^2=1\), the (independent) AR(1) processes \(\xi_{1t}\) and \(\xi_{2t}\) with AR(1)-coefficients of 0.9 and 0.6, respectively.







As an example, in the bivariate example above, if \((1, -b)\) is a CI-vector, then any multiple \((c, -cb)\) is also a CI-vector, as the linear combination remains stationary.
Why this matters? Because of this non-uniqueness, software (like R or EViews) usually reports ‘’normalized’’ cointegrating vectors. They typically set the first coefficient to 1 (just as we did with above for \(y_{1t}\)) to make the results interpretable.

title: 11  Cointegration
text:
11.2 Cointegrated VAR and VECM model
Consider the \(K\)-dimensional VAR(\(p\)) process \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{x}_{t} = \boldsymbol{A}_{1} \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}+\cdots+ \boldsymbol{A}_{p} \boldsymbol{x}_{t-p} + \boldsymbol{u}_{t}, \quad t=1,2,...
\end{equation*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{u}_{t}\sim\mathsf{iid}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_u)\).
First rewrite the model using the lag polynomial \(\boldsymbol{A}(\mathsf{B}) = \boldsymbol{I}_{K} - \boldsymbol{A}_{1}\mathsf{B}-\cdots-\boldsymbol{A}_{p}\mathsf{B}^{p}\). Using the algebraic result on lag polynomials (see Appendix A) similar to the univariate unit root case, we can decompose it as: \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{A}\left(\mathsf{B}\right) = \boldsymbol{A} \left(1\right)\mathsf{B} + \left(\boldsymbol{I}_{K}-\sum_{j=1}^{p-1} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{j}\mathsf{B}^{j}\right)\Delta,
\end{equation*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{j} = -\boldsymbol{A}_{j+1}-\cdots - \boldsymbol{A}_{p}\). Substituting this back allows us to write the VAR(\(p\)) as a Vector Error Correction Model (VECM) presentation: \[\begin{equation*}
    \Delta \boldsymbol{x}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\Theta} \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^{p-1} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{j} \Delta \boldsymbol{x}_{t-j} + \boldsymbol{u}_{t}, \quad t=1,2,...  
\end{equation*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\Theta} =-\boldsymbol{A}(1)\).
 
The reduced rank condition. Now, assume that the standard stationarity condition (\(\det(\boldsymbol{A}(z))\neq 0\) for all \(\left\vert z\right\vert\leq 1\)) does not hold. Instead, assume the polynomial \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}(z))\) has roots at \(z=1\) (unit roots).

Consequently, \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}(1))=0\), which implies that the matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) is singular (reduced rank). Let the rank of \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) be \(r < K\), that is, \(\mathsf{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Theta})=r\).

Using a standard result from matrix algebra, any (\(K \times K\)) matrix of rank \(r\) can be decomposed into the product of two \(K \times r\) matrices of rank \(r\): \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{\Theta} = \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime},
\end{equation*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) are \((K\times r)\) matrices with \(\mathsf{rank}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\mathsf{rank}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=r\). Plugging this into the above model equation yields the VECM model: \[\begin{equation*}
    \Delta \boldsymbol{x}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^{p-1} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{j} \Delta \boldsymbol{x}_{t-j} + \boldsymbol{u}_{t}, \quad t=1,2,...  
\end{equation*}\]
Interpretation: If we assume that \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t} \sim I(1)\), and \(\mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t})= \boldsymbol{0}\), then the term \(\Delta \boldsymbol{x}_{t}\) is stationary (\(I(0)\)). Since the error term \(\boldsymbol{u}_{t}\) is also \(I(0)\), for the equation to balance, the term \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}\) must also be stationary (\(I(0)\)). This implies that the process \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}\) is cointegrated.
Cointegrating vectors. The columns of the matrix \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) are the cointegrating vectors. The linear combinations \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}\) represent deviations from the long-run equilibrium relationships between the components of \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}\).

These deviations are called “equilibrium errors”.
Since equilibrium errors are stationary, they fluctuate randomly around zero with constant variance. Once the system deviates from equilibrium, it tends to return to it.

Adjustment matrix. The parameter \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) is often called the adjustment matrix (or loading/weight matrix).

It describes how the errors \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}\) feed back into the system to affect the changes \(\Delta \boldsymbol{x}_{t}\).
Essentially, \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) determines the speed and direction of the correction mechanism that forces the non-stationary variables back toward their equilibrium relationship.

 
Example case: A simple VECM presentation of the VAR(2) model. The bivariate cointegrated VAR(2) model with one cointegrating vector (\(r = 1\)) has the following VECM representation \[\begin{eqnarray*}
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\Delta x_{1t} \\
\Delta x_{2t} \end{array} \right] &=&
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\alpha_1   \\
\alpha_2   \end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{cc}
\beta_1   & \beta_2 \\
\end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c}
x_{1, t-1} \\
x_{2, t-1} \end{array} \right] +
\left[ \begin{array}{cc}
\lambda_{11,1} & \lambda_{12,1}  \\
\lambda_{21,1} & \lambda_{22,1}  \end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\Delta x_{1, t-1} \\
\Delta x_{2, t-1} \end{array} \right] +
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
u_{1t} \\
u_{2t} \end{array} \right] \\
&=&
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\alpha_1 (\beta_1 x_{1, t-1} + \beta_2 x_{2, t-1})   \\
\alpha_2 (\beta_1 x_{1, t-1} + \beta_2 x_{2, t-1})  \end{array} \right]
+
\left[ \begin{array}{cc}
\lambda_{11,1} & \lambda_{12,1}  \\
\lambda_{21,1} & \lambda_{22,1}  \end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\Delta x_{1, t-1} \\
\Delta x_{2, t-1} \end{array} \right] +
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
u_{1t} \\
u_{2t} \end{array} \right].
\end{eqnarray*}\]

 
The Granger Representation Theorem. In the derivation above, we assumed \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t} \sim I(1)\). The connection between the unit root assumption in \(\boldsymbol{A}(1)\) and the VECM representation is formalized by the Granger Representation Theorem.

Details are beyond the scope of this course.


 
Impulse responses in cointegrated systems. In the context of a stationary VAR process, impulse response functions are based on the coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{j}\) of the VMA(\(\infty\)) representation. While an \(I(1)\) process does not have a standard VMA(\(\infty\)) representation, we can still define the impulse responses using the same recursive logic.
For a stationary VAR, the coefficient matrices are computed as: \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{\Psi}_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{j} \boldsymbol{\Psi}_{j-i} \boldsymbol{A}_{i},\ \boldsymbol{\Psi}_{0}=\boldsymbol{I}_{K},\ j=1,2,...,
\end{equation*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{A}_{i}=\boldsymbol{0}\) when \(i>p\). This formula remains well-defined even if the starting point is a cointegrated VAR(\(p\)) process \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}\). However, there is a fundamental difference in behavior:

Stationary case: Impulse responses converge to zero as \(j \to \infty\).
Integrated (\(I(1)\)) case: The impulse responses do not converge to zero but instead usually converge towards a nonzero constant. This reflects the “permanent” nature of shocks in non-stationary cases. Consequently, the “total impact” (sum of matrix coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j\)) often defined for stationary VARs cannot be defined for the \(I(1)\) case, but the impulse response analysis itself remains a useful tool.

 
Adding Deterministic Terms. In the derivations above, we assumed the stationary components had zero mean, which is rarely realistic. We now extend the VECM to include deterministic terms like constants and trends.
Case 1: Nonzero mean. Consider the process \(\boldsymbol{y}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \boldsymbol{x}_{t}\), where \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}\) follows a VAR(\(p\)) and satisfies the Granger Representation Theorem. The resulting VECM is: \[\begin{equation*}
    \Delta \boldsymbol{y}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\alpha} \left(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{y}_{t-1}-\boldsymbol{\nu}\right) + \sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{j}\Delta \boldsymbol{y}_{t-j} + \boldsymbol{u}_{t},
\end{equation*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\nu} = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{\mu}\).

Interpretation: The term \(\boldsymbol{\nu}\) represents the expectation of the stationary linear combinations. The system corrects towards the equilibrium \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{y}_{t-1} = \boldsymbol{\nu}\).

Case 2: Linear trend. A more general model includes a linear trend: \(\boldsymbol{y}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_{0} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_{1}t + \boldsymbol{x}_{t}\). The corresponding VECM is: \[\begin{equation*}
    \Delta \boldsymbol{y}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\nu}_{0} + \boldsymbol{\alpha} \left(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{y}_{t-1}-\boldsymbol{\nu}_{1}(t-1)\right) + \sum_{j=1}^{p-1} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{j} \Delta \boldsymbol{y}_{t-j} + \boldsymbol{u}_{t},
\end{equation*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\nu}_{1} = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1}\).

In this general specification, the linear combinations \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{y}_{t}\) are not stationary because their expectation contains a linear trend component.


Restricted trend: An important special case arises if \(\boldsymbol{\nu}_{1} = \boldsymbol{0}\), simplifying the model to: \[\begin{equation*}
    \Delta \boldsymbol{y}_{t} = \boldsymbol{\nu}_{0} + \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{y}_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^{p-1} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{j} \Delta \boldsymbol{y}_{t-j} + \boldsymbol{u}_{t}.
\end{equation*}\] Here, the cointegrating relations \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{y}_{t-1}\) are stationary around a constant, even though the variables \(\boldsymbol{y}_{t}\) themselves drift with a linear trend.

title: 11  Cointegration
text:
11.3 Cointegration relations and identification
As discussed, cointegrating vectors are not unique: if the \(r \times K\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime}\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{y}_t \sim I(0)\), then \(\boldsymbol{C} \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{y}_t\) is also \(I(0)\) for any non-singular \(r \times r\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{C}\). To interpret the model, we must impose restrictions or normalization to achieve identification.
Because the cointegrating matrix \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is not uniquely determined, we must impose restrictions to identify the parameters. A standard approach is the normalization strategy.
We begin by partitioning the \(K\)-dimensional vector of variables \(\boldsymbol{y}_t\) into two groups: \[\begin{equation*}
\boldsymbol{y}_t = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \boldsymbol{z}_t \\ \boldsymbol{q}_t \end{array} \right],
\end{equation*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{z}_t\) is \(r \times 1\) and \(\boldsymbol{q}_t\) is \((K-r) \times 1\).
A common identification assumption is to normalize \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) such that the first \(r\) rows form an identity matrix: \[\begin{equation*}
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} = [\boldsymbol{I}_r \quad : \quad \boldsymbol{A}],
\end{equation*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{I}_r\) is an \(r \times r\) identity matrix and \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is an \(r \times (K-r)\) matrix of coefficients to be estimated. Key statistical implications:

Linear independence: This normalization is valid if and only if the \(r\) variables chosen for \(\boldsymbol{z}_t\) are linearly independent in the cointegration space. Mathematically, the \(r \times r\) sub-matrix of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) corresponding to the variables in \(\boldsymbol{z}_t\) must be non-singular (invertible).
Common stochastic trends: In a system with \(K\) variables and \(r\) cointegrating equations, there are exactly \(K-r\) independent sources of non-stationarity. These are known as the common stochastic trends. By partitioning the model this way, we treat the sub-process \(\boldsymbol{q}_t\) as the “engine” of the system; it contains the \(K-r\) trends that drive the long-run path of the entire vector.
Economic interpretation: This structure often aligns with economic theories where \(r\) variables (in \(\boldsymbol{z}_t\)) adjust to an equilibrium determined by the remaining \(K-r\) variables (in \(\boldsymbol{q}_t\)).

For example, if \(r=1\), we can express the long-run relation as: \[\begin{equation*}
z_{1,t} = -a_{11}q_{1,t} - a_{12}q_{2,t} \dots + \text{error}_t
\end{equation*}\] Here, \(z_{1,t}\) ‘’follows’’ the stochastic trends generated by the \(\boldsymbol{q}_t\) variables. If the ‘’drivers’’ in \(\boldsymbol{q}_t\) shift, \(z_{1,t}\) must eventually adjust to maintain the equilibrium.


Estimation and inference. The asymptotic theory for \(I(1)\) processes is non-standard. However, standard procedures exist for VECM estimation.

Assuming the cointegrating rank \(r\) is known, the VECM parameters can be estimated using maximum likelihood (Johansen’s Reduced Rank Regression). This method can also handle models with specific structural restrictions on the cointegrating vectors.
Lag length selection: Typically, one first selects the lag length \(p\) for the unrestricted VAR (in levels) using information criteria (AIC, BIC, HQ) or sequential testing, and then estimates the VECM with \(p-1\) lags in differences.

Hypothesis testing: Once the model is estimated and identified (e.g., using the normalization \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} = [\boldsymbol{I}_r \, : \, \boldsymbol{A}]\)):

t-tests: The standard \(t\)-test can be used to evaluate the significance of individual coefficients in \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) or the non-restricted part of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) (\(\boldsymbol{A}\)), as these estimates are asymptotically normal.
Wald tests: Hypotheses restricting multiple parameters simultaneously can be tested using the Wald test statistic, which follows an asymptotic \(\chi^2\)-distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of restrictions.

Diagnostic checks: Standard diagnostic checks used for stationary VAR models (e.g., Portmanteau tests for residual autocorrelation, ARCH-LM tests for heteroskedasticity) are also applicable to VECMs. Additionally, plotting the estimated cointegration relations—the residuals \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{y}_t\)—provides visual verification that the relations are indeed stationary.

title: 11  Cointegration
text:
11.4 Testing cointegration
Determining the number of cointegration relationships is of particular interest in different applications.
Engle-Granger approach. At times the cointegration vector is known based on some (economic) theory.

See, e.g., the previous examples on the consumption-income relationship.

In this case, construct the cointegration relationship \(z_t = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime} \boldsymbol{y}_t\) and test whether the null hypothesis of no cointegration will be rejected.
If it is known that there exists at most one cointegrating vector, a simple approach to test for the existence of cointegration is the Engle-Granger approach.

Run a (linear) regression of \(y_{1t}\) (the first element of \(\boldsymbol{y}_t\)) on the other \(K-1\) variables \(y_{2t}, \ldots, y_{Kt}\) and testing the unit root in the residuals.
This is based on the idea of the normalization introduced above.
Unit root testing can be based on the ADF test (critical values are, however, different!). If the unit root hypothesis is rejected, the hypothesis of no-cointegration is also rejected.

The above static regression gives consistent estimates of the cointegrating vector.

In a second stage, the error-correction model can be estimated using the estimated cointegrating vector from the first stage.

There are, however, problems with this Engle-Granger approach:

The results of the tests are sensitive to the left-hand side variable of the regression, that is, to the normalization applied to the cointegrating vector.
If the cointegrating vector happens not to involve \(y_{1t}\) but only \(y_{2t}, \ldots, y_{Kt}\), the above test is not appropriate.
The residual-based test tends to lack power because it does not exploit all the available information about the dynamic interactions of the variables.
More than one cointegrating relationship may exist.

 
Johansen approach. An alternative approach (that does not suffer from the above drawbacks) was proposed by Johansen (1988), who developed a maximum likelihood estimation procedure.

This also allows one to test for the number of cointegrating relations.
The details of the Johansen procedure are complex and we shall only focus on the main aspects (for empirical analysis).

The first step in the Johansen approach involves testing hypotheses about the rank of the long-run matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\), or equivalently the number of columns in \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) (\(K \times r\)).

Imposing the restriction \(\boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\prime}\) and for a given \(r\), it can be shown that the maximum likelihood estimate for \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) in the VECM equals the matrix containing the \(r\) eigenvectors corresponding to the \(r\) largest (estimated) eigenvalues of a \(K \times r\) matrix.

Let us denote the (theoretical) eigenvalues of this matrix in decreasing order as \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \, \cdots \, \ge \lambda_K\).

If there are \(r\) cointegrating relationships (and \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) has rank \(r\)), it must be the case that \(\mathrm{log} (1-\lambda_j) = 0\) for the smallest \(K-r\) eigenvalues, that is, for \(j = r+1,r+2, \ldots, K\).

(Johansen approach): trace test
We can use the (estimated) eigenvalues \(\widehat{\lambda}_1 > \widehat{\lambda}_2 > \, \cdots \, > \widehat{\lambda}_K\) to test hypotheses about the rank of \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\).
For example, the hypothesis \(H_0: r \le r_0\) against \(H_1: r_0 < r \le K\) can be tested using the likelihood ratio (LR) test statistic \[\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{LR} = - T \sum_{j=r_0+1}^{K} \mathrm{log} (1-\widehat{\lambda}_j).
\end{equation*}\] Trace test checks whether the smallest \(K-r_0\) eigenvalues are significantly different from zero.

The trace (and the following maximum eigenvalue) test statistic has generally a nonstandard asymptotic null distribution (do not have the usual \(\chi^2\)-distribution).

(Johansen approach): maximum eigenvalue test
We can test \(H_0: r \le r_0\) against \(H_1: r = r_0+1\) using the maximum eigenvalue test statistic \[\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{LR}_{max} = - T \, \mathrm{log} (1-\widehat{\lambda}_{r_0+1}).
\end{equation*}\]
It is based on the estimated \((r_0 +1)\)th largest eigenvalue.
As with the unit root tests, the null distributions of both the trace and maximum eigenvalue tests depend on the fact whether a constant (and a time trend) are included in.
 
Determining the cointegrating rank. The cointegration rank may be specified by means of a sequential testing procedure, starting from a test of no cointegration (\(r = 0\) or rank(\(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\)) = 0) up to a test of full stationarity (\(r = K\) or rank(\(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\)) = \(K\)).
The full sequence of hypotheses is \[\begin{eqnarray*}
H_0(0) &:& \mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}) = 0 \,\, \mathrm{vs} \,\, H_1:\mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}) > 0 \\
H_0(1) &:& \mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}) = 1 \,\, \mathrm{vs} \,\, H_1:\mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}) > 1 \\
& \vdots &  \\
H_0(K-1) &:& \mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}) = K-1 \,\, \mathrm{vs} \,\, H_1:\mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Theta})=K.
\end{eqnarray*}\] Each hypothesis can be tested by the trace or the maximum eigenvalue test. The testing sequence terminates, and the corresponding cointegrating rank is selected, when the null hypothesis cannot be rejected for the first time.

If the first hypothesis, \(H_0(0)\), cannot be rejected, a VAR model for the differenced series is considered.
Rejection of all the hypotheses implies a VAR model for the levels.

title: 12  Big Dependent Data
text:
12.1 Background
So far, we have examined standard VAR model (and its VECM counterpart). In practice, the number of variables in these models must be kept relatively small to maintain estimation accuracy and efficiency. Models with more than, say, six variables are rare. However, especially in many economic applications, this dimensionality constraint presents significant challenges.
Omitted variable bias. In applications where the underlying dynamics are driven by a large information set, restricting the model to a handful of variables creates a substantial risk of omitted variable bias.
Unobserved variables. Economic theory or other background information (or equivalent results in other application fields) often features variables that lack precise empirical counterparts or are measured with error.
Modelling specific dynamics. Standard VARs focus on varying a few key aggregates. However, researchers are often interested in the dynamic reaction of specific, disaggregated variables (e.g., sector-specific prices or regional housing starts). Including all these variables in a standard VAR is computationally infeasible.
The FAVAR solution. One solution to these dimensionality problems, within the VAR context, is the Factor Augmented Vector Autoregression (FAVAR) model. The core idea is to utilize a large dataset (where even the number of variables \(M\) may exceed the number of observations \(T\)) to construct a small number of common factors via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and then include these factors in the VAR model.
The FAVAR approach offers distinct advantages:
In the following sections, we will focus first on extracting factors from large datasets and second on utilizing them in the VAR analysis. This discussion draws heavily on Chapter 16 of Kilian and Lütkepohl (2017).

title: 12  Big Dependent Data
text:
For example, central banks monitor hundreds of variables when conducting monetary policy. Excluding this information from a model can lead to distorted results.
A classic example is the “price puzzle” observed in early VAR-based monetary policy literature, where a contractionary monetary policy shock appeared to increase the price level. This counter-intuitive result is widely attributed to omitted variable bias: if the model does not include forward-looking inflation expectations (which the central bank observes), it misinterprets a policy rate hike—enacted in anticipation of future inflation—as the cause of the subsequent price rise.



For instance, “inflation” is a theoretical concept representing the decline in the value of money. In practice, we observe proxies like the Consumer Price Index (CPI) or core inflation (excluding volatile energy and food prices).
It is often unclear which specific proxy best represents the underlying theoretical variable. A factor model approach allows us to extract the common signal (the underlying inflation) from a large panel of different price indicators.






Dimension reduction: It condenses the information from hundreds of variables into a few factors, keeping the parameter space manageable.
Proxies for unobservables: Factors can act as better proxies for theoretical concepts (like “economic activity” or “global financial cycle”) than any single observed variable.
Broader analysis: It allows for the analysis of shocks (in structural VARs) on a vast set of variables that are not explicitly in the VAR system but are part of the large dataset used to extract factors.



Note: The notation in this chapter differs slightly from previous sections. Specifically, matrices and dimensions here relate to large-scale factor methods and should not be confused, for example, with notation in the previous cointegration and VECM section.

title: 12  Big Dependent Data
text:
12.2 Factor models
Static factor model
Let \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) be an \(M \times 1\) vector of observed, demeaned variables. We assume these variables are driven by a small number of unobserved common factors \(\boldsymbol{f}_t\) (\(r \times 1\)) and idiosyncratic errors. The static factor model is defined as: \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{x}_t = \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \boldsymbol{f}_t + \boldsymbol{v}_t,
\end{equation*}\] where

\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) is the (\(M \times r\)) matrix of factor loadings.
\(\boldsymbol{v}_t \sim \mathsf{iid}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_v)\) is the vector of idiosyncratic errors.

We assume that the common factors and idiosyncratic errors are uncorrelated, i.e., \(\mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{v}_s \boldsymbol{f}_t^\prime) = \boldsymbol{0}\) for all \(s, t\). Typically, we assume \(M \gg r\). The covariance matrix of \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) implies: \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x = \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_f \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^\prime + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_v.
\end{equation*}\] This model is not uniquely identified without further restrictions. Common identification assumptions include:

Orthogonal loadings: \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^\prime \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \boldsymbol{I}_r\).
Uncorrelated, standardized factors: \(\boldsymbol{f}_t \sim (\boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{I}_r)\), implying \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_f\) is a diagonal matrix.

 
Estimation via PCA
If \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) were known, we could estimate the factors easily. In practice, we estimate the factors by maximizing the variance of \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) explained by the common component (equivalently, minimizing the variance of the idiosyncratic errors). The objective function is: \[\begin{equation*}
    \min_{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}, \boldsymbol{f}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{f}_T} \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\boldsymbol{x}_t-\boldsymbol{\Lambda} \boldsymbol{f}_t)^\prime (\boldsymbol{x}_t-\boldsymbol{\Lambda} \boldsymbol{f}_t).
\end{equation*}\] The solution is found via Principal Component Analysis (PCA):

Find the \(r\) largest eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 > \dots > \lambda_r\) of the sample covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{S}_x = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\boldsymbol{x}_t \boldsymbol{x}_t^\prime\) and their corresponding (orthonormal) eigenvectors \(\bar{\lambda}_1, \dots, \bar{\lambda}_r\).
Set the estimated loading matrix is \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}} = [\bar{\lambda}_1, \dots, \bar{\lambda}_r]\).
The estimated factors are \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{f}}_t = \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}^\prime \boldsymbol{x}_t\).

The eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) represent the empirical variance explained by the \(i\)-th factor, ordered from largest to smallest.
 
Dynamic factor model
The static model assumes factors and errors are serially uncorrelated. The Dynamic Factor Model (DFM) generalizes this by allowing for autoregressive dynamics: \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{x}_t = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^f \boldsymbol{f}_t + \boldsymbol{v}_t,
\end{equation*}\] where the factors and errors follow time-series processes: \[\begin{align*}
    \boldsymbol{f}_t &= \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1 \boldsymbol{f}_{t-1} + \cdots + \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s \boldsymbol{f}_{t-s} + \boldsymbol{\eta}_t, \\
    \boldsymbol{v}_t &= \boldsymbol{A}_1 \boldsymbol{v}_{t-1} + \cdots + \boldsymbol{A}_p \boldsymbol{v}_{t-p} + \boldsymbol{u}_t.
\end{align*}\] Here \(\boldsymbol{A}_i\) are typically diagonal matrices, and \(\boldsymbol{u}_t\) is white noise (or iid) error term.
 
Note: We assume \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) is stationary. While factor models exist for integrated processes, the methods presented here assume stationarity.
 
Dynamic form. If \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) depends directly on lagged values of the factors, we obtain the dynamic form of the model: \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{x}_t = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_0^f \boldsymbol{f}_t + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1^f \boldsymbol{f}_{t-1} + \cdots + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{q^*}^f \boldsymbol{f}_{t-q^*} + \boldsymbol{v}_t.
\end{equation*}\] Assuming the same DGP for \(\boldsymbol{f}_t\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_t\) as in the static form (as above) of the DFM, this model can be written in lag operator notation as \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{x}_t = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^f(\mathsf{B}) \boldsymbol{f}_t + \boldsymbol{v}_t, \quad \boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\mathsf{B}) \boldsymbol{f}_t = \boldsymbol{\eta}_t, \quad \boldsymbol{A}(\mathsf{B}) \boldsymbol{v}_t = \boldsymbol{u}_t
\end{equation*}\] where \[\begin{eqnarray*}
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^f(\mathsf{B}) &=&  \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_0^f  + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1^f \mathsf{B} + \cdots + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{q^*}^f \mathsf{B}^{q^*}, \\
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\mathsf{B}) &=& \boldsymbol{I}_r - \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_1 \mathsf{B}- \cdots - \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s \mathsf{B}^s, \\
\boldsymbol{A}(\mathsf{B}) &=& \mathrm{diag}\Big[a_1(\mathsf{B}) \, \cdots \, a_M(\mathsf{B}) \Big],
\end{eqnarray*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{v}_t\) is the vector of idiosyncratic components, and \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_t\) is white noise or iid error term such that \(\mathsf{E}(\boldsymbol{u}_t \boldsymbol{\eta}^{\prime}_s) = \boldsymbol{0} \, \forall t,s\)).
Interestingly, this dynamic form can be rewritten in a static representation by stacking the current and lagged factors into a larger vector \(\boldsymbol{F}_t = (\boldsymbol{f}_t^\prime, \ldots, \boldsymbol{f}_{t-q^*}^\prime)\). The observation equation becomes \[\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{x}_t = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^F \boldsymbol{F}_t + \boldsymbol{v}_t,
\end{equation*}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^F = \Big[\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_0^f \quad \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1^f \quad \cdots \quad \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{q^*}^f \Big]\). This allows us to estimate the dynamic model using the PCA approach described for the static model.
Estimation strategy. Recall that the model can be rewritten as \[\begin{equation*}
   \boldsymbol{A}(\mathsf{B}) \boldsymbol{x}_t = \boldsymbol{A}(\mathsf{B}) \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^f(\mathsf{B}) \boldsymbol{f}_t + \boldsymbol{u}_t.
\end{equation*}\] A recommended iterative procedure for estimating the DFM (see Stock and Watson, 2005):

Initialize: Estimate univariate AR models for each component of \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) to get initial estimates \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{A}}(\mathsf{B})\).
PCA step: Estimate factors \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{F}}_t\) from the filtered model \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{A}}(\mathsf{B}) \boldsymbol{x}_t\) using PCA.
Regression step: Estimate the factor loadings and error dynamics by regressing \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) on the estimated factors.
Iterate: Repeat steps 2 and 3 until convergence.

 
Choosing the number of factors. Since PCA does not rely on the time structure, a common heuristic for selecting \(r\) (the number of factors) is the scree plot approach or a variance threshold. One specifies a target fraction of total variance (e.g., 50% or 90%) and selects the minimum number of principal components required to explain that cumulative variance.
Asymptotic convergence. Standard theory suggests estimation improves as \(M \to \infty\). However, Boivin and Ng (2006) highlight that simply adding more data is not always beneficial if the new variables have correlated errors or weak factor loadings. Quality matters more than quantity; including noisy or irrelevant variables can degrade the precision of factor estimates.

13  Predictive regressions with time series variables
text:
13.1 Linear regressions containing I(1) variables
In this section, we focus on predicting (univariate) \(y_{t+h}\) at the time \(t\) (forecast origin) given the collection of \(K\) predictive variables in \(\boldsymbol{x}_t = (x_{1t},\ldots,x_{Kt})\), which may also contain some lagged values of \(y_t\). The general predictive regression model is given by: \[\begin{equation*}
y_{t+h} = \boldsymbol{x}^{\prime}_t \boldsymbol{\beta} + u_{t+h} = \sum_{i=1}^{K} x_{it} \beta_i + u_{t+h}, \quad t=1,\ldots, T-h.
\end{equation*}\] where the forecast horizon \(h\) is given and fixed, \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is the vector of parameters and \(u_{t+h}\) is the error term with typical assumptions (such as an \(\mathsf{iid}\) error term).
Standard assumption: Stationarity. Unless otherwise specified, in the general predictive regression framework, we assume that the variables included in \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) and the dependent variable \(y_t\) are stationary.
We consider two major deviations from this standard framework below
Consider the linear regression \[\begin{equation*}
y_t= \boldsymbol{x}^{\prime}_t \boldsymbol{\beta} + u_t,
\end{equation*}\] and the two assumptions \(\mathrm{(i)}\)–\(\mathrm{(ii)}\):
Assume now that only \(\mathrm{(i)}\) holds, that is the error term \(u_t\) is serially uncorrelated and uncorrelated with the regressors included in \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\).
To examine these points in more detail, let us consider again the following relatively simple regression model \[\begin{equation*}
y_t= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{t-1} + \beta_2 x_{t-2} + u_t,
\end{equation*}\] where \(x_t \thicksim I(1)\). The model can be rewritten as \[\begin{equation*}
y_t= \beta_0 + (\beta_1+\beta_2) x_{t-1} - \beta_2 (x_{t-1} - x_{t-2}) + u_t,
\end{equation*}\] or \[\begin{equation*}
y_t= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (x_{t-1}-x_{t-2}) + (\beta_1 + \beta_2) x_{t-2} + u_t.
\end{equation*}\] As \((x_{t-1} - x_{t-2}) \thicksim I(0)\), and hence, standard inference on \(\beta_2\) (or \(\beta_1\)) holds. Therefore, both \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) cannot simultaneously be written as coefficients of \(I(0)\) variables (unless higher lags are included in the model).
Let us continue with the above linear regression where now also the assumption \(\mathrm{(i)}\) does not hold and the dependent variable is \(I(1)\).
The complete cheat sheet on linear regression with \(I(0)\) and \(I(1)\) variables is summarized hereby:
A spurious regression emerges when a statistically significant relationship between two \(I(1)\) variables \(y_t\) and \(x_t\) is found although those are completely unrelated. Assume that a researcher estimates a linear regression \[\begin{equation*}
y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + u_t,
\end{equation*}\] but assuming wrongly that the variables \(y_t\) and \(x_t\) are stationary. Instead, they are generated by two independent random walks (i.e., \(y_t\) and \(x_t\) are \(I(1)\) variables) \[\begin{eqnarray*}
y_t &=& y_{t-1} + u_{1t}, \quad u_{1t} \thicksim \mathsf{iid}(0, \sigma^2_1), \\
x_t &=& x_{t-1} + u_{2t}, \quad u_{2t} \thicksim \mathsf{iid}(0, \sigma^2_2).
\end{eqnarray*}\] This typically leads to the estimation result of the above linear regression characterized by a fairly high \(R^2\) (the coefficient of determination), highly autocorrelated residuals \(\widehat{u}_t\) and a (highly) statistically significant estimate of \(\beta_1\). This result is clearly spurious given that the variables are completely independent!
Solution to this problem is to include the lags of \(y_t\) and \(x_t\) as predictors in the model. In other words, we end up a model \[\begin{equation*}
y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + \beta_2 y_{t-1} + \beta_3 x_{t-1} +  u_t.
\end{equation*}\] In this case the OLS estimator is consistent. Thus, in general, including lagged values in the regression is sufficient to solve many of the problems associated with possibly spurious regressions.

\(\mathrm{(i)}\) The error term \(u_t\) is serially uncorrelated and uncorrelated with the regressors included in \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\).
\(\mathrm{(ii)}\) All the regressors in \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) are either deterministic or stationary random variables.



Even if the model cannot be written in this way, the OLS estimator of the coefficients of the \(I(1)\) regressors \(\boldsymbol{x}_t\) is consistent. However, its asymptotic distribution is, in general, nonstandard such that usual inference does not apply.
If the model can be written such that all the parameters of interest are coefficients of mean zero stationary variables, their OLS estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal.



The OLS estimator of \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) is not, in general, jointly asymptotically normal.
The test statistic on a hypothesis concerning both coefficients (for instance \(H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2\)), in general, does not have the usual asymptotic \(\chi^2\)-distribution.




If the dependent variable is not cointegrated with any of the regressors, the OLS estimator of the coefficients of the \(I(1)\) regressors is inconsistent.
If the dependent variable is cointegrated with at least one of the regressors, the OLS estimator of the parameters of interest

that can be written as coefficients of stationary variables, is inconsistent.
that cannot be written as coefficients of stationary variables, is consistent, but not asymptotically normal.

For instance, consider the following regression model: \[\begin{equation*}
y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1t} + \beta_2 x_{2t} + u_t,
\end{equation*}\] where all variables are \(I(1)\), and \(y_t\) and \(x_{2t}\) are cointegrated and assumption \(\mathrm{(i)}\) does not hold.

If \(x_{1t}\) and \(x_{2t}\) are cointegrated such that \((x_{1t} - \gamma x_{2t}) \thicksim ~ I(0)\), the model can be written as \[\begin{equation*}
y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (x_{1t} - \gamma x_{2t}) + (\beta_1 \gamma + \beta_2) x_{2t} + u_t,
\end{equation*}\] and the OLS estimator of \(\beta_1\) is inconsistent.
If \(x_{1t}\) is not cointegrated with \(x_{2t}\), \(\beta_1\) cannot be written as a coefficient of an \(I(0)\) variable, and hence, its OLS estimator is consistent, but not asymptotically normal.

Estimation results like this should not be taken seriously.
The reason is that with \(y_t\) and \(x_t\) being \(I(1)\) variables, the error term \(u_t\) will also be \(I(1)\), not stationary (\(I(0)\)).
